summary.text: Zooxanthellae are photosynthetic single-celled organisms that live in symbiosis with marine invertebrates such as corals, jellyfish, sponges and nudibranchs.
By day they pass products of photosynthesis to their host, sometimes meeting up to 90% of its energy needs for metabolism, growth and reproduction.
In return they receive nutrients, carbon dioxide and a raised spot with access to sunlight, and their pigments give many hosts a yellowish or brownish colour.

facts.value: Sea anemones, jellyfish, giant clams, sponges, flatworms

items.prompt: Living inside a host animal, up to what share of its energy needs can zooxanthellae supply?

options.label: About 5%
About 30%
Up to 90%

items.explain: Through photosynthesis they sometimes provide up to 90% of the host's energy for metabolism, growth and reproduction.

items.prompt: A coral full of zooxanthellae is kept in a completely dark tank. What do its partners lose the ability to do?

options.label: Swim from one coral to another
Make food for the coral by photosynthesis

items.explain: Zooxanthellae are photosynthetic, and the food they give their host comes from photosynthesis, which needs sunlight.

items.prompt: Zooxanthellae feed their host. What does the host give them back?

options.label: Nutrients, carbon dioxide and access to sunlight
Oxygen and a dark place to hide from light
Ready-made sugars from the host's meals

items.explain: In return for photosynthesis products, they receive nutrients, carbon dioxide and an elevated position with access to sunlight.

items.prompt: How did zooxanthellae first come to live inside host cells?

options.label: They forced their way in as parasites
They grew out of the host's own cell parts
Hosts farmed them on their outer skin first
Hosts took them in but failed to digest them

items.explain: Host cell lysosomes took them up, but instead of being broken down they survived because they supplied carbon compounds to the host.

items.prompt: Many corals and sea anemones look yellowish or brown. Where do those colours mostly come from?

options.label: Mud and sand stuck to the animal
Rust from iron dissolved in seawater
Pigments in the zooxanthellae inside them
The host's own blood showing through

items.explain: Zooxanthellae contain pigments such as peridinin and diadinoxanthin that give the yellowish and brownish colours typical of many hosts.

options.label: The giant clam Tridacna
The great white shark
The green sea turtle
The bottlenose dolphin

items.explain: Besides reef-building corals, their hosts include sea anemones, jellyfish, nudibranchs, sponges, flatworms and bivalves such as the giant clam Tridacna.

paragraphs.heading: What they are
paragraphs.text: Zooxanthellae is an informal name for single-celled organisms that make food from sunlight and can live in partnership with sea animals such as corals, jellyfish, sponges and nudibranchs. Most known kinds belong to the dinoflagellate genus Symbiodinium, though some are known from the genus Amphidinium. Other groups, not yet identified, may form similar partnerships too. The name means little yellow animal. Karl Brandt first used it in 1881.

paragraphs.heading: A fair trade
paragraphs.text: During the day, zooxanthellae pass their host some of what they make by photosynthesis, at times meeting up to 90% of its energy needs for metabolism, growth and reproduction. In return, the host gives them nutrients, carbon dioxide and a raised spot with access to sunlight. They are best known from reef-building corals, but they also live in many sea anemones, giant clams, flatworms and other hosts.

paragraphs.heading: Origins and colour
paragraphs.text: The partnership began when host cells took in dinoflagellate cells through their lysosomes. Rather than being broken down, the swallowed cells survived, because they gave the host a supply of carbon compounds. Their pigments, chlorophyll a and c along with peridinin and diadinoxanthin, give many host animals their yellowish and brownish colours.

paragraphs.heading: Inside the cell
paragraphs.text: Each cell holds chloroplasts whose thylakoids sit in clusters of three, and each chloroplast has a pyrenoid sticking out of it, wrapped in a thick, starchy coat. The DNA is packed into tight coils of chromatin in the nucleus. Like all other dinoflagellates, zooxanthellae carry 5-hydroxymethyluracil and thymidine in their genomes, something no other eukaryotic genome has.

paragraphs.heading: A changing life
paragraphs.text: Zooxanthellae switch between cysts and forms that move through the water. Their main form is the vegetative cell, which has a thin wall and either splits into two daughter cells or becomes a cyst. Cysts have thick walls, make up most of the zooxanthellae clustered in host tissue, and give the host a reddish-brown hue. Dividing cysts, in which two daughter cells stay joined, make up about a quarter of those clusters.

paragraphs.heading: The swimming stage
paragraphs.text: A much rarer stage can swim. It begins as a zoosporangium and matures into a zoospore, and only zooxanthellae that start as zoospores can move. A zoospore either swims forward, spinning around the axis of its rear flagellum, or gyrates while that flagellum is attached to a surface. This swimming cell makes and releases gametes for reproduction.
